I have everything I need: the full text of the blog post plus the accompanying quickstart README, which describes the harness that was eventually built around the failure. The source is a narrative engineering write-up rather than a single logged trajectory, so the account below is drawn from the behaviors the post describes, and I'll flag where the post gives detail versus where it only summarizes.

## Source

Anthropic Engineering, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents," by Justin Young, published Nov 26, 2025 — https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents. Accompanying code: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-quickstarts/tree/main/autonomous-coding.

## Setup: the task and the agent

- **Agent:** Claude Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK. The SDK provided standard coding tools (bash, file read/write) and context management via compaction. Later iterations added a Puppeteer MCP server for browser automation.
- **Task:** A single high-level prompt — the post's example is "build a clone of claude.ai" — to be carried out by running the agent in a loop across many context windows. The post describes this as work spanning "hours, or even days." The quickstart README puts a session at 5–15 minutes and a full build at "many hours" across sessions.
- **Structure of the run:** The agent works in discrete sessions. Each new session begins with a fresh context window and "no memory of what came before," apart from whatever compaction summaries and on-disk artifacts exist. The post's analogy: engineers working in shifts where each arriving engineer has no memory of the prior shift.
- **Baseline condition ("out of the box"):** No initializer prompt, no feature list, no progress file, no init.sh. The agent simply received the high-level prompt and was looped, relying on compaction to bridge context windows.

## What happened, in order

The post says that under the baseline condition, "even a frontier coding model like Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows will fall short of building a production-quality web app." The failures came in a chronological sequence over the life of the project:

### 1. Early in the project: the agent tries to build everything at once

In the first sessions, given only the high-level prompt, the agent "tended to try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app." Rather than picking a slice of functionality, it began implementing broadly.

**Feedback signal received:** none that changed behavior. The agent kept implementing until the context window filled up. The post states this "often led to the model running out of context in the middle of its implementation."

**Observable state left behind:** a feature "half-implemented and undocumented." No commit boundaries, no notes describing what was finished versus in flight.

### 2. Next session: the successor agent inherits a broken, undocumented environment

A new session starts with a fresh context. The post notes that compaction was in effect but "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent" — so the summary the new session received did not reliably describe what the previous one had been in the middle of.

**What the agent did:** It "would then have to guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again." The post describes this explicitly as time spent recovering a working baseline rather than advancing the project. The post also notes that without an init.sh script the agent had to "spend time figuring out how to run the app" every session — a related recurring cost, which the failure-modes table lists as its own row.

### 3. Later in the project: a session declares the job done

Once some features had actually been built, a different pattern appeared. The post: "After some features had already been built, a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done."

**Signal that triggered this:** the visible presence of existing working code. There was no artifact enumerating what "done" meant for the full prompt, so the agent judged completeness from what it could see in the repo and ended the session — leaving the project incomplete relative to a "production-quality" claude.ai clone.

### 4. Throughout: features marked complete without end-to-end verification

The post calls this "one final major failure mode." Absent explicit prompting, Claude "tended to make code changes, and even do testing with unit tests or curl commands against a development server, but would fail [to] recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end."

So the agent *did* test — unit tests, curl against the dev server — and received passing signals from those checks. It then treated the feature as done. The verification it ran did not exercise the feature the way a user would (through the browser UI), and the feature was nonetheless recorded as working.

### 5. Residual issue even after the fix: alert modals invisible to the agent

After the team added the Puppeteer MCP server and instructed Claude to "do all testing as a human user would," the post says Claude "mostly did well at verifying features end-to-end." One remaining gap is documented: "Claude can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, and features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result." That is, the agent's browser-based verification returned no signal for alert dialogs, and features depending on them were marked passing while still buggy.

## Final outcome of the baseline run

The post does not give a single terminal state for one specific trajectory. What it states is that the looped baseline agent "will fall short of building a production-quality web app," with the project cycling through: broad partial implementations → context exhaustion mid-feature → successor sessions spending time re-establishing a working app → later sessions prematurely declaring completion → features recorded as done that did not work end-to-end.

## What was changed in response (for context only, not analysis)

The post's remedy — documented so the failure account has its counterfactual — was a two-part harness with an identical system prompt, tools, and harness but different *initial user prompts* (footnote 1):

- **Initializer agent (session 1):** expands the prompt into a JSON `feature_list.json` of 200+ features, each with steps and `"passes": false`; writes `init.sh` to start the dev server; writes `claude-progress.txt`; makes an initial git commit.
- **Coding agent (sessions 2+):** runs `pwd`, reads `claude-progress.txt` and `feature_list.json`, reads `git log --oneline -20`, runs `init.sh`, does a basic end-to-end smoke test via Puppeteer (start a new chat, send a message, receive a response), then picks *one* failing feature, implements it, verifies it in the browser, flips only its `passes` field, commits with a descriptive message, and appends to the progress file.
- The feature list is JSON specifically because "the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown," and the prompt includes "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality."

The post's own summary table lists four failure modes: declaring victory too early; leaving the environment with bugs or undocumented progress; marking features done prematurely; and spending time figuring out how to run the app.

## Caveats about the source

This is a summary write-up, not a raw trajectory. It reports behavior in aggregate ("tended to," "often," "would often occur later"), does not give session counts, token counts, or a specific run's transcript for the *failing* baseline. The only transcript-like excerpt provided is of the *fixed* harness's typical session opening. There is also a minor inconsistency to note: the post's example transcript refers to a `tests.json` file while the rest of the post and the quickstart use `feature_list.json`; and the quickstart's default model is `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` while the post's baseline observation is about Opus 4.5.

Effective harnesses for long-running agents

Published Nov 26, 2025
Agents still face challenges working across many context windows. We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents.

As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem.
The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions.
We developed a two-fold solution to enable the Claude Agent SDK to work effectively across many context windows: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session. You can find code examples in the accompanying quickstart.
The long-running agent problem
The Claude Agent SDK is a powerful, general-purpose agent harness adept at coding, as well as other tasks that require the model to use tools to gather context, plan, and execute. It has context management capabilities such as compaction, which enables an agent to work on a task without exhausting the context window. # Autonomous Coding Agent Demo

A minimal harness demonstrating long-running autonomous coding with the Claude Agent SDK. This demo implements a two-agent pattern (initializer + coding agent) that can build complete applications over multiple sessions.

## Prerequisites

**Required:** Install the latest versions of both Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK:

```bash
# Install Claude Code CLI (latest version required)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# Install Python dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Verify your installations:
```bash
claude --version  # Should be latest version
pip show claude-code-sdk  # Check SDK is installed
```

**API Key:** Set your Anthropic API key:
```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='your-api-key-here'
```

## Quick Start

```bash
python autonomous_agent_demo.py --project-dir ./my_project
```

For testing with limited iterations:
```bash
python autonomous_agent_demo.py --project-dir ./my_project --max-iterations 3
```

## Important Timing Expectations

> **Warning: This demo takes a long time to run!**

- **First session (initialization):** The agent generates a `feature_list.json` with 200 test cases. This takes several minutes and may appear to hang - this is normal. The agent is writing out all the features.

- **Subsequent sessions:** Each coding iteration can take **5-15 minutes** depending on complexity.

- **Full app:** Building all 200 features typically requires **many hours** of total runtime across multiple sessions.

**Tip:** The 200 features parameter in the prompts is designed for comprehensive coverage. If you want faster demos, you can modify `prompts/initializer_prompt.md` to reduce the feature count (e.g., 20-50 features for a quicker demo).
